title: Why Chatbots Make Things Up
objective: After this level you can explain why a language model can state false things fluently, and check a chatbot's answer against a source.
summary: A language model writes likely text, so it can confabulate: state falsehoods confidently, even fake citations. The check that works is a source outside the chatbot.

cards.headline: A lawyer asked the chatbot: is this case real? It said yes.
cards.body: In the 2023 Mata v. Avianca case, lawyers filed a brief citing court cases that ChatGPT had made up. One lawyer asked ChatGPT whether a case was real, and it said the case existed. It didn't. Why would a machine vouch for something it invented?

cards.headline: Likely is not the same as true
cards.body: NIST's name for this is confabulation: confidently stated but false content, often called hallucinations. It's a natural result of how these models work: they produce text that fits the statistical patterns of their training data, one likely token after another. Level 7's adder gets 1 + 1 = 10 by fixed rules. Picking a likely next token follows no such rule for truth.

cards.headline: Why guess instead of saying "I don't know"?
cards.body: A 2025 research paper offered one explanation. Like students facing a hard exam, models guess when they're unsure, because training and most evaluations reward guessing over admitting uncertainty. On a test graded only right or wrong, a blank scores nothing and a guess sometimes scores. So a confident wrong answer can look better on paper than an honest "I don't know."

cards.headline: Check outside the chatbot
cards.body: NIST warns that these models can produce made-up citations that appear to back up an answer. So asking the chatbot "are you sure?" just asks the same guesser again. The check that works is outside it: find the source yourself and see that it exists and says what was claimed. The lawyer did search a free site for the case. He couldn't find it, and cited it anyway.

mascot.line: Keep this: a chatbot checking itself isn't a check. The source has to exist outside it.

cards.headline: Made-up answers: explained
learned: Models produce likely text, not checked text
Tests that reward guessing encourage bluffing
Check the source yourself, outside the chatbot

questions.prompt: When generative AI confidently presents false content, NIST calls it _____.

options.label: compression
options.rationale: Compression shrinks data; it has nothing to do with truth.

options.label: overfitting
options.rationale: Overfitting is memorizing a training set.

options.label: encryption
options.rationale: Encryption scrambles data to keep it secret.

questions.explanation: NIST calls it confabulation: confidently stated but erroneous or false content, often called hallucinations.

questions.prompt: A binary adder turns 1 + 1 into 10 every time by fixed rules. Why can a chatbot state a false fact just as confidently?

options.label: The adders inside its chips are broken and add numbers wrongly
options.rationale: The hardware adds correctly; the text is predicted.

options.label: It writes text that fits patterns in its data, true or not
Its makers told it to mislead people on purpose
options.rationale: Confabulation is a natural result of prediction, not an order.

options.label: It looks up every fact but misreads it
options.rationale: It predicts likely tokens rather than looking facts up.

questions.explanation: Generative models produce text that fits the statistical patterns of their training data, which can be false yet sound sure.
